references.text: In the previous verse, the rich man asks Abraham to send Lazarus to his father's house. Verse 28 continues with the reasoning: he has five brothers whom he wants to warn, so that they too do not come to this place of torment ([ref:Luk 16:27|Luke 16:27]).

Abraham answers the rich man's request by pointing out that his brothers have Moses and the Prophets to listen to, and that even if someone rose from the dead, they would not be convinced – a testimony to the sufficiency of Scripture ([ref:Luk 16:29-31|Luke 16:29-31]).
Peter's exhortation to be saved from this perverse generation reflects the same motive: to warn others so that they do not perish ([ref:Apg 2:40|Acts 2:40]).

Paul testified to both Jews and Greeks about repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus, an expression of the same desire to warn people as the rich man wished for his brothers ([ref:Apg 20:21|Acts 20:21]).

Paul declares that he is innocent of everyone's blood because he has not held back anything from God's counsel – the motive of testifying and warning others so that they may avoid destruction ([ref:Apg 20:26-27|Acts 20:26-27]).

Paul urged each one as a father urges his children, so that they would walk in a manner worthy of God – this reflects the urgent warning the rich man wished to send to his brothers ([ref:1 Tess 2:11-12|1 Thessalonians 2:11-12]).

The prophet Ezekiel was commissioned to warn the wicked, so that he might turn and live. The rich man's desire to warn his brothers reflects this prophetic calling ([ref:Esek 3:18-19|Ezekiel 3:18-19]).
Jeremiah brought forward God's warning to a people who would not listen, paralleling the desire to testify so that people do not end in destruction ([ref:Jer 42:5-6|Jeremiah 42:5-6]).
Jude urges others to snatch people from the fire with fear – the same concern for others' eternal fate as the rich man expressed toward his brothers ([ref:Jud 1:23|Jude 1:23]).
